question: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test always detects it when present and has a 5% false-positive rate. A randomly chosen person tests positive. Is the probability they have the disease above 50%?

claims.text: The probability of disease given a positive test is about 2%, not above 50%.
The test has 100% sensitivity and never misses a true case.
A 5% false-positive rate sounds small, so a positive result seems like strong evidence of disease.
The disease is rare (1 in 1,000), so most people who test positive are healthy.
Among 100,000 people, about 100 are sick and all test positive.
About 4,995 of the 99,900 healthy people test positive falsely.
Roughly 5,095 test positive and only about 1.96% of them have the disease.
The base rate is the deciding factor, with false positives outnumbering true positives about 50 to 1.
